content:
Many supplements are marketed for joint health. This guide sets out what the evidence does and does not show, so you can decide whether a supplement is worth discussing with a pharmacist or GP. It does not recommend any brand or product.

Quick answer: Supplement evidence for arthritis is limited and mixed. NICE advises against offering glucosamine for osteoarthritis because there is no strong evidence of benefit. Small trials of turmeric (curcumin) and ginger suggest a possible modest effect on pain, but they do not show these are as effective as anti-inflammatory medicines. Vitamin D is advised for general health in the UK, not as an arthritis treatment. Check with a pharmacist or GP before starting any supplement, especially if you take other medicines.

What NICE says

The NICE osteoarthritis guideline (NG226) says not to offer glucosamine to manage osteoarthritis, and to explain that there is no strong evidence of benefit if someone asks about it. The core treatments NICE recommends are therapeutic exercise, information and support, and help with weight loss where relevant.

Common supplements and the evidence

Omega-3 fish oils

Some studies suggest fish oils may slightly help joint symptoms in rheumatoid arthritis, but the evidence is uncertain and fish oils are not a replacement for prescribed treatment. Eating oily fish as part of a balanced diet is advised for general health by the NHS. Fish oil can affect bleeding risk, so check with a pharmacist if you take blood thinners.

Turmeric (curcumin)

Small, short trials suggest curcumin may modestly reduce osteoarthritis pain in some people. The studies were small and varied in quality, so they do not show curcumin works as well as anti-inflammatory medicines. Turmeric supplements can interact with some medicines, including blood thinners, and liver problems have been reported with some products. Talk to a pharmacist before trying it.

Ginger

Reviews of small trials suggest ginger may give a small reduction in osteoarthritis pain, but results are inconsistent. It may also interact with blood thinners.

Vitamin D

The NHS advises everyone in the UK to consider 10 micrograms of vitamin D a day in autumn and winter, and some people all year round. This is for general bone and muscle health; it is not a treatment for arthritis. Do not take more than the NHS upper limit unless a doctor advises it.

Glucosamine and chondroitin

Trial results are inconsistent, and NICE advises against offering glucosamine for osteoarthritis. Most glucosamine is made from shellfish, so it may not be suitable if you have a shellfish allergy.

Collagen

Evidence for collagen supplements is very limited. There is no reliable evidence that they repair cartilage or change how arthritis progresses.

Before you buy

  • Supplements cannot cure arthritis or rebuild cartilage.
  • Ask a pharmacist to check for interactions with your other medicines.
  • Tell your GP or rheumatology team what you take, especially before surgery.
  • Look for the Traditional Herbal Registration (THR) mark on herbal products, which shows the product meets MHRA quality standards. It does not prove the product works.
  • Stop and seek advice if you get side effects.

Frequently asked questions

What is the best supplement for arthritis?

No supplement has strong evidence of benefit. Exercise, weight management where relevant, and treatment agreed with your healthcare team have the best support.

Is turmeric as good as ibuprofen?

The evidence does not show this. Trials were small and short.
